2 Methods for Sequence Processing using usearch11


USEARCH version v11.0.667_i86osx64

usearch v11.0.667_i86osx64, 68.7Gb RAM, 16 cores

Note that all steps were performed separately for the 16S and ITS datasets

Step 1: Merge paired-end reads


Flags 16S value ITS value Explanation
-fastq_pctid 90 90 Minimum %id of alignment
-fastq_maxdiffs 20 20 Maximum number of mismatches in the alignment.
-fastq_trunctail 30 30 Truncate reads at the first Q score with <= this value.
-fastq_minmergelen 150 150 Minimum length for the merged sequence.
-fastq_minovlen 25 25 Discard pair if alignment is shorter than given value.


Same flags for 16S and ITS

for i in *_R1.fastq
  do
 usearch -fastq_mergepairs $i -fastq_pctid 90 -fastq_maxdiffs 20 -fastq_trunctail 30 -fastq_minmergelen 150 -relabel ${i:0:9}. -fastqout 2_ReadProcessing/16S_merged/${i:0:9}_merged.fastq
  done

Flags 16S value ITS value Explanation
-stripleft 17 18 removes n letters at the start of a sequence
-stripright 21 20 removes n letters at the end of a sequence 
for i in *_merged.fastq
  do
 usearch -fastx_truncate $i -stripleft 17 -stripright 13 -fastqout 2_ReadProcessing/16S_filtered/${i:0:9}_filtered.fastq
  done

Step 3: QC by max EE and minimum length filtering

Phred scores
Next-generation reads specify a Phred score for each base, also known as a Quality or Q score. Q=20 corresponds to an error probability of 1%.

Expected number of errors
Assume that the Phred scores are good, in other words assume that the machine makes good estimates of the error probabilities. Now we can measure the overall quality of a read by calculating the expected number of errors in the read. The Q scores can’t tell us exactly how many errors there are in a given read. However, the Q scores can tell us what the average number of errors would be in that large collection, and this is the definition of the expected number of errors. Because we’re taking an average, the value is real rather than integer, and can be less than one. To calculate the expected number of errors: it is the sum of the error probabilities.

Choosing the maximum expected error threshold
A natural choice is E_max = 1, because the most probable number of errors of a filtered read is zero.

When to QC

Our paired read merger (assembler) reported re-calculated Phred scores in the overlapping region to reflect that we have two independent observations of the same bases. If the forward and reverse read agree on a base, then our confidence that the base is correct should increase. Quality filtering by maximum expected errors should be performed as a post-processing step after reads have been merged in order to take advantage of the re-calculated Phred scores, which should be better predictions of the true error rates.

Flags 16S value ITS value Explanation
-fastq_maxee 1.0 1.0 Discard reads with > E total expected errors for all bases in the read after any truncation options have been applied.
-fastq_minlen 240 240 Discard sequences with < L letters. 
for i in *_filtered.fastq
  do
 usearch -fastq_filter $i -fastq_maxee 1.0 -fastq_minlen 240 -fastaout 2_ReadProcessing/16S_qcd/${i:0:9}_qcd.fasta
  done

Step 7: Map trimmed reads to the representative OTU sequences in each dataset


The reads we are mapping are the output of step 2: the paired-end reads have been merged and the primers truncated, but the reads have not been quality filtered yet. Note that sequences across all samples have been concatenated into 1 file and the fasta headers reflect the sample id. The representative OTU sequence is the most abundance sequence in an OTU cluster.

usearch -otutab 2_ReadProcessing/16S_filtered_all.fastq -otus 3_OTUs/16S_OTUs/16S_individ_otus.fa -otutabout 3_OTUs/16S_OTUs/16S_otutab_kf.txt -mapout 3_OTUs/16S_OTUs/16S_map_kf.txt
